head: Password manager hacked: what a breach can and can't expose
dek: When a password manager company is hacked, your saved passwords stay locked as long as the vault is encrypted with a key only you hold, but your name, email and other account details can still leak and lead to targeted phishing.

p: On 25 November 2026, 1Password said an attacker had got into an employee's work GitHub account. The company started investigating on 19 November. The attacker reached source code, pushed malicious code to backend services and copied account records for some customers.

Those records held names, email addresses, account and user IDs, the dates accounts were created and last signed in, public keys, and tokens in some invitation, provisioning and recovery emails. 1Password says vault contents, the keys that protect vaults and account recovery keys weren't accessed, and its apps and browser extensions weren't affected.

sections.h: How a vault stays locked when the company is hacked
p: Most password managers encrypt your vault on your own device before it is uploaded. 1Password's security page says everything in an account is end-to-end encrypted with AES-GCM-256. The key comes from your account password combined with a 128-bit Secret Key, and the company says your account password is never stored with your data or sent over the network.

Bitwarden describes the same idea as zero knowledge: its help page says vault data is encrypted before it is stored anywhere, its servers only hold encrypted data, and you are the only party with the keys to decrypt it. So a copy of the servers' data is, in theory, a pile of locked boxes. 1Password's incident post says the same holds for an attacker who gets into its servers.

sections.h: What still leaks: the parts that aren't encrypted
p: Not everything in an account is inside the vault. Billing details, your name, your email address and sign-in times sit with the company, and that is what the 1Password attacker took. With that, someone can write you an email that looks real and mentions your actual account.

Some services also leave parts of the vault itself unencrypted. In LastPass's incident, reported on 22 December 2022, an attacker copied a backup of customer vaults. LastPass said website addresses in it were not encrypted, while user names, passwords, secure notes and form-fill data were encrypted with 256-bit AES. Basic account details such as names, billing addresses, email and phone numbers and IP addresses were copied too.

sections.h: When your master password matters most
p: A stolen encrypted vault can be attacked offline, guess after guess, so the strength of the password that unlocks it decides how long it holds. LastPass said in 2022 that customers whose master password met its defaults, at least 12 characters with 100,100 PBKDF2 rounds, didn't need to act. It told everyone else to change the passwords of the websites stored in their vault.
1Password adds the Secret Key, which you never type into a website and the company doesn't store. On 25 November, it told customers that they didn't need to change anything in their accounts.

sections.h: The real risk after a breach: fake messages
p: With names and emails in an attacker's hands, the next step is usually phishing. 1Password asked customers to be wary of unexpected emails, texts or calls about 1Password, invitations or account recovery that they didn't start. It says it will never ask for your account password or Secret Key, and that you should type them only into its own app or website.
As a precaution, 1Password made the codes in invitation and recovery emails ten characters long instead of six digits, rotated internal credentials and brought in outside security experts.

means: If your password manager's company is breached, your saved passwords are protected by the vault's encryption and your master password, but expect convincing fake emails that use your real name and account details.
todo: Read the company's own incident page, not a forwarded email, and follow what it says. Make sure your master password is long and used nowhere else. Never type your master password, Secret Key or recovery code into a page you reached from a message; open the app or type the address yourself. If the company says vaults were copied, change the passwords for your important accounts first.
